solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One hitting photographer, young and cocky

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a young and cocky person; the clue gives the adjectives describing one

blocks.note: one who whips is one hitting
a snapper is informal for a photographer, one who takes snaps

explanation.surface: A brash young press photographer lashing out at someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One hitting photographer' reads as a single phrase about an assault, but splits into two job titles that join into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippersnapper is a presumptuous, impertinent young person, so the term labels someone both youthful and overconfident.

clue.text: A minor hum — faulty instrument

indicators.note: something faulty is not working properly, so the letters before it are out of order

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A small hum in A minor reveals a broken musical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonium is a small reed organ played with a keyboard, a musical instrument.

clue.text: Joke I caught referring to Carthage

blocks.note: a pun is a joke on words
taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to a quip about ancient Carthage.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket scoring, c marks a batsman caught out.
explanation.definitionFit: Punic is the adjective for ancient Carthage and its people, as in the Punic Wars against Rome.

clue.text: Eat this perhaps in exotic hacienda surrrounding lake?

definitions.note: a description of the answer: a food you might eat

indicators.note: exotic means strange and foreign, so these letters appear in an unfamiliar order
surrounding means going round, so the letters wrap around the abbreviation for lake

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
L is the usual abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A meal on a ranch near a lake in some foreign land.
explanation.walkthrough: A hacienda is a Spanish or Latin American estate, which suits the Mexican dish. 'Surrounding' is misspelt with three Rs in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchilada is a Mexican tortilla rolled round a filling, so it is something you might eat.

clue.text: Quiet — quite so on regular basis, stops trading maybe

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so every other letter of the phrase is kept

blocks.note: sh is the call for quiet
second, fourth and sixth letters of this phrase

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper quietly agrees that business is regularly halting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuts' in the sense of a shop closing for the day, hence the 'maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop that shuts closes and stops doing business, at least for the day.

clue.text: Sports title with cash involved

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and complicated, so these letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Money becoming tangled up with sporting championships.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletics is the collective name for running, jumping and throwing events, a group of sports.

clue.text: Best part to begin with, ample

indicators.note: to begin with points to the start, so only the first letter of the word before is used

blocks.note: a plum job or role is the best one
first letter of this word

explanation.surface: The best role starts out generous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best part' looks like one phrase but splits: the first word gives the fruit, the second only its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Plump and ample both describe a full, rounded figure, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Think female put out by English being put in office again

indicators.note: being put out by another means being ousted and replaced by it

blocks.note: to reflect is to think
F is the abbreviation for female
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A woman displaced by an Englishman as someone wins office a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: The F of the thinking word is swapped for an E.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-elect someone is to vote them back into the post they held, so they are put into office once more.

clue.text: State mineral used up (almost)

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the phrase is lost

blocks.note: ore is a mineral that is mined
used up means gone, here without its final letter

explanation.surface: A US state whose mineral deposits are nearly exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' is not a verb here but one of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregon is a state in the north-western United States, on the Pacific coast.

clue.text: Err badly having Greek character back for second performance

indicators.note: doing something badly means getting it wrong, so the letters come out in a muddled order
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the Greek letter is read right to left

blocks.note: taken as written, before being rearranged
nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: An actor makes a mess of a Greek role and has to perform the scene again.
explanation.definitionFit: A rerun is a repeat showing, so it is a performance given a second time.

clue.text: Where players meet audience after bash

indicators.note: placing one thing after another fixes the order, so the audience word goes second

blocks.note: to club someone is to bash them
a theatre's house is its audience, as in 'a full house'

explanation.surface: A troupe gathering with their audience after a lively party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the audience word second. 'Bash' looks like a noun for a party but works as the verb to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A clubhouse is the building at a sports ground where team members gather and change, so it is a meeting place for sportspeople.

clue.text: Pasta almost gone somehow, initially causing concern — hotel intervenes

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
somehow suggests things arranged in some unspecified way, so the remaining letters are jumbled
initially points to the beginnings, so only the first letter of each following word is kept
something that intervenes comes between other things, so the hotel letter is placed inside

blocks.note: the word gone without its last letter
first letters of these two words
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
first letter of this word, which also signals the insertion

explanation.surface: Someone worried that the pasta has nearly run out, while a hotel steps in to help.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged remnant of gone is followed by the initials of causing, concern and intervenes; H then sits between the Cs and the I. The final I has to come from intervenes doing double duty, a loose point in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnocchi are small Italian dumplings usually classed with pasta, made from potato or semolina dough.

clue.text: Expensive, the Parisian church feature

blocks.note: a steep price is an expensive one
le is French for 'the', as a Parisian would say it

explanation.surface: A tourist finds a Paris church's famous feature pricey to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Parisian' means 'the' in French, not a person from Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall tower and spire rising from a church, one of its most visible architectural parts.

clue.text: Northern tune originally arranged for money

indicators.note: originally refers to the origin or start, so only the first letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for northern
an air is a melody or tune
first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A northern folk melody first arranged to earn some cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The naira is the national currency of Nigeria, so it is a unit of money.

clue.text: Quite a few intended, we hear, to create growth area

indicators.note: we hear means the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

blocks.note: quite a few is a lot, and intended is meant

explanation.surface: A lot of people planned to set up an area for development.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment is a small rented plot of land in Britain where people grow vegetables. 'Growth area' sounds like economics, but means somewhere things grow.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is a council garden plot for cultivating plants, literally an area for growing things.

clue.text: Captain flexible about place? Hopeful

indicators.note: something flexible can be bent into another shape, so these letters are rearranged
about means going around, so the captain's letters wrap the abbreviation for place

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
PL is the usual abbreviation for place, as in street names

explanation.surface: A team captain is open-minded about where to play, hopeful of selection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hopeful' is a noun here, as in 'presidential hopefuls'. The abbreviation joins the captain's letters before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An applicant is someone applying for a post, and a hopeful is a candidate seeking success, so the nouns overlap.

clue.text: Trophy in France for Rhode Island collection?

blocks.note: pot is slang for a sports trophy, a cup
pour is French for 'for'
RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: A cup won in France on behalf of an American state's team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' tells you to translate the word that follows into French.
explanation.definitionFit: A potpourri is a mixture or medley, and in its looser sense any miscellaneous collection of things.

clue.text: Pole here using tactic, ran amok

indicators.note: running amok is wild, disorderly behaviour, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it is fodder as well as part of the signal phrase

explanation.surface: A Polish visitor using a wild strategy that gets out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person but is the South Pole, which lies in the region described.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antarctic is the region around the South Pole, so it is where that pole is found.

clue.text: Following rules, slight switch in protest

indicators.note: a small swap of position means two letters of the next word trade places

blocks.note: a complaint is a protest

explanation.surface: Someone keeping to the regulations while lodging only a mild protest.
explanation.walkthrough: Only two adjacent letters, the A and I, swap places: a minimal change that turns a grumble into obedience.
explanation.definitionFit: Compliant describes someone who obeys or conforms, which is exactly what following rules means.

clue.text: Ship, one moving quickly

blocks.note: first meaning: a fast sailing vessel of the nineteenth century
second meaning: someone or something that goes at a clip, a fast mover

explanation.walkthrough: The two parts read as one description of a fast ship, but they are separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A clipper was a sleek, fast merchant ship, and the word also means anything that moves at a rapid clip.

clue.text: With no introduction, use sheep in arrangement

indicators.note: lacking an introduction means the word is missing its opening letter

blocks.note: the word use without its first letter
a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: A farmer, without preamble, puts the flock to work in some scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a dialect word for a ram, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A setup is the way something is organised or arranged, as in the office setup.

clue.text: Favour quiet whistleblower, hero at heart

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: p is piano, the musical marking for quiet
a referee blows the whistle in a match
the two central letters of this word

explanation.surface: Supporting a discreet whistleblower who is a hero deep down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistleblower' suggests someone exposing wrongdoing, but here it is the match official.
explanation.definitionFit: To prefer something is to like it better or favour it over other options.

clue.text: Home at six with type of shirt for guest

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
VI is six in Roman numerals
a tee is a T-shirt

explanation.surface: Being home at six o'clock in the right shirt to receive a visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' simply sits between the first two pieces as part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An invitee is a person who has been invited, which is what a guest is.

clue.text: Elvis, talented (just a bit!). That's nice to see

indicators.note: just a bit means only a small portion of the words is used, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A modest verdict on the King's talent, then a remark on a pleasant sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A vista is a pleasing view or prospect, something agreeable to look at.

clue.text: Best fare, ultimately low in calories

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: last letter of this word
lite is the trade spelling of light, used for low-calorie products

explanation.surface: The finest food turns out to be a diet option.
explanation.definitionFit: The elite are the best of a group, the pick of the bunch.

clue.text: Pay special attention to former pupil — wait

blocks.note: OB is short for old boy, a former pupil of a school
to wait at table is to serve

explanation.surface: An old school pupil is told to look carefully and be patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old boy' is the British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe is to watch or heed closely, so it means giving something particular attention.

clue.text: Leave dessert

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for to depart quickly
second meaning: a banana sundae of ice cream and fruit

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to skip pudding; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: To split is slang for leaving, and a banana split is a classic dessert, often called just a split.

clue.text: Behind advertisement, one not half poor

indicators.note: not half means only half the word survives, here its second pair of letters

blocks.note: a poster is a printed advertisement
I is the Roman numeral for one
the second half of this word

explanation.surface: Behind a billboard someone sits who is hardly penniless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like a preposition but is the noun for one's rear. 'Not half' is also a British phrase meaning 'very much'.
explanation.definitionFit: Posterior is a jocular noun for the buttocks, which is also what a behind is.

clue.text: Drink after hours, entertaining time

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so this word holds another inside it

blocks.note: after hours is late
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Having a drink late at night while having a fun time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After hours' is not the link 'after' but the whole time phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is a coffee made with steamed milk, so it is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Acid retort, hate, sadly — make dissatisifaction clear

indicators.note: sadly means in a sorry state, so these words are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A bitter reply and some hatred, regrettably voicing displeasure.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act was a 1714 British law read aloud to order crowds to disperse; the phrase now means to reprimand severely.
explanation.definitionFit: To read someone the riot act is to scold them firmly, an idiom for showing your displeasure.
